title: Treacle Tart
subtitle: golden syrup and breadcrumb tart with a crisp shortcrust shell
excerpt: Treacle tart is one of Britain's most beloved puddings. The filling is just golden syrup, breadcrumbs, and lemon -- simple, intensely sweet, and very satisfying. Serve with clotted cream or cold custard.
sourceNotes: A classic British tart. The name is misleading -- despite the name, it is made with golden syrup rather than black treacle.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the pastry case a day ahead. Fill and bake on the day.

content.text: Warm the golden syrup briefly before mixing in the breadcrumbs -- it becomes much easier to pour and stir. The lemon juice is not optional; without it the sweetness becomes one-dimensional. Use fresh white breadcrumbs, not dried, for the best texture.

items.prepNote: fresh white breadcrumbs are better if available

content.text: Rub the butter into the flour until it resembles fine breadcrumbs. Add 2 to 3 tablespoons of cold water and bring together into a disc. Chill for 30 minutes.

Heat the oven to 200C. Roll the pastry to 3mm and line a 23cm loose-bottomed tart tin. Trim the edges, prick the base, and blind bake for 12 minutes. Remove the baking beans and bake for 5 more minutes. Reduce the oven to 180C.
Warm the golden syrup in a saucepan over low heat until runny. Remove from heat. Stir in the breadcrumbs, lemon zest, and lemon juice. Mix well.
Pour the filling into the pastry case. Bake at 180C for 25 to 30 minutes until the filling is just set and lightly coloured. It will firm up as it cools.
Leave to cool in the tin for at least 20 minutes before removing. Serve warm or at room temperature.

items.cause: Under-baked, or cut while still very hot.
items.fix: Give it the full 30 minutes. The filling sets properly as it cools. Do not cut until it is barely warm.

items.cause: Too many breadcrumbs relative to syrup.
items.fix: The ratio in this recipe is correct. If using very dry dried breadcrumbs, use 130g instead of 150g.

content.text: Treacle tart is a school dinner and Sunday lunch pudding with deep roots in British food culture. Golden syrup was introduced to British kitchens in the 1880s and quickly became a staple in baking. The tart appears at every level of British cooking -- from school canteens to restaurant dessert menus. It is unpretentious and very, very good.
